name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q01 - Scope of chemical thermodynamics and reaction rate

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Chemical thermodynamics deals with macroscopic systems, focusing on the interconversions of heat and other forms of energy, the overall energy changes accompanying a process, the feasibility (spontaneity) of a chemical reaction, and the extent to which the reaction proceeds before reaching equilibrium.

Evaluation of Scope
Thermodynamics is concerned solely with the initial and final states of a system at equilibrium. It provides no information regarding the time taken for a change, the reaction mechanism, or the rate (speed) at which reactants convert into products. The speed and mechanism of a chemical process are governed strictly by chemical kinetics.

Final Conclusion
Therefore, thermodynamics is not concerned about the rate at which a reaction proceeds.

answer.text: energy changes involved in a chemical reaction.
the extent to which a chemical reaction proceeds.
the rate at which a reaction proceeds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q02 - Definition and example of closed thermodynamic system

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic systems are classified based on the exchange of matter and energy with their surroundings:

  • An open system can exchange both energy and matter with surroundings.
  • A closed system can exchange energy (heat and work) across its boundary, but cannot exchange matter with surroundings.
  • An isolated system can exchange neither energy nor matter with surroundings.

Evaluation of Systems
A covered beaker prevents the transfer of matter, making it a closed system rather than an open system. In a closed system, matter cannot be transferred; only energy is exchanged. A sealed vessel made of copper possesses rigid, thermally conducting (diathermic) walls: matter cannot enter or leave the vessel, but heat energy can readily pass through the copper boundary to and from the surroundings. Thus, reactants inside a closed copper vessel represent a closed system. A thermos flask or insulated vessel has adiabatic boundaries preventing heat exchange as well as matter exchange, representing an isolated system.

Final Conclusion
The correct statement is that the presence of reactants in a closed vessel made up of copper is an example of a closed system.

answer.text: The presence of reacting species in a covered beaker is an example of open system.
There is an exchange of energy as well as matter between the system and the surroundings in a closed system.
The presence of reactants in a closed vessel made up of copper is an example of a closed system.
The presence of reactants in a thermos flask or any other closed insulated vessel is an example of a closed system.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q03 - State variables describing the state of gas

questiontext.text: The state of a gas can be described by quoting the relationship between____.

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The thermodynamic state of a macroscopic gaseous system is completely specified by macroscopic state variables or state functions. For a given sample of gas, these fundamental parameters are pressure \(p\), volume \(V\), absolute temperature \(T\), and the amount of substance (number of moles) \(n\).

Equation of State
An equation of state relates these variables to one another, such that specifying any three automatically determines the fourth (for example, the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\)). Thus, describing the thermodynamic state requires quoting the relationship among all four variables: pressure, volume, temperature, and amount.

Final Conclusion
The state of a gas is described by quoting the relationship between pressure, volume, temperature, amount.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q04 - Specific heat capacity upon reducing gas volume

questiontext.text: The volume of gas is reduced to half from its original volume. The specific heat will be ____.

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Specific heat capacity is defined as the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of a substance by one unit of temperature (\(1\text{ K}\) or \(1\;^{\circ}\text{C}\)): \[ c = \frac{C}{m} = \frac{q}{m\Delta T} \] where \(C\) is the total heat capacity and \(m\) is the mass of the substance.

Evaluation of Intensive Property
Specific heat capacity is an intensive property because it is the ratio of two extensive properties (heat capacity and mass). Intensive properties depend solely on the chemical nature and temperature of the substance and are completely independent of the quantity, mass, or volume of the sample present.

Final Conclusion
Because specific heat is an intensive property, reducing the volume of the gas to half leaves its specific heat unaltered. The specific heat will remain constant.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q05 - Thermochemical reaction for complete combustion of butane

questiontext.text: During complete combustion of one mole of butane, \(2658\text{ kJ}\) of heat is released. The thermochemical reaction for above change is

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Substance undergoing combustion: \(1\text{ mol}\) of butane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}(g)\).
Heat released during complete combustion: \(2658\text{ kJ}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By IUPAC convention, when heat is evolved by the reacting system (exothermic reaction), the enthalpy change of combustion \(\Delta_c H\) carries a negative sign: \[ \Delta_c H = -2658.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \] Standard states of reactants and products at \(298\text{ K}\) are \(\mathrm{CO_2}(g)\) and liquid water, \(\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
The standard enthalpy of combustion is defined per mole of combustible substance. The balanced stoichiometric equation for the combustion of \(1\text{ mole}\) of butane \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}(g)\) is: \[ \mathrm{C_4H_{10}}(g) + \frac{13}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{CO_2}(g) + 5\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \]

Step-by-Step Working
Combining the stoichiometric reaction per mole of butane with the measured enthalpy change: \[ \mathrm{C_4H_{10}}(g) + \frac{13}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{CO_2}(g) + 5\mathrm{H_2O}(l); \quad \Delta_c H = -2658.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \]

Check and Final Answer
Water in its thermodynamic reference standard state at room temperature is in liquid form \(\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\), not steam \(\mathrm{H_2O}(g)\), and the stoichiometric coefficient of butane must be \(1\). Hence, the correct thermochemical reaction is: \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}(g) + \frac{13}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{CO_2}(g) + 5\mathrm{H_2O}(l); \quad \Delta_c H = -2658.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q06 - Relationship between enthalpy and internal energy of formation

questiontext.text: \(\Delta_{f}U^{\ominus}\) of formation of \(\mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{g})\) at certain temperature is \(-393\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). The value of \(\Delta_{f}H^{\ominus}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Internal energy change of formation: \(\Delta_f U^{\ominus} = -393\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Species formed: \(1\text{ mol}\) of methane gas, \(\mathrm{CH}_4(g)\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The standard formation reaction forms one mole of the substance from its constituent elements in their most stable reference states at the given temperature: \[ \mathrm{C}(\text{graphite}, s) + 2\mathrm{H}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_4(g) \]

Relevant Formulae and Principles
The relationship between enthalpy of reaction \(\Delta H\) and internal energy change \(\Delta U\) for a gaseous reaction is: \[ \Delta_f H^{\ominus} = \Delta_f U^{\ominus} + \Delta n_g RT \] where \(\Delta n_g\) represents the change in the number of moles of gaseous species: \[ \Delta n_g = n_g(\text{products}) - n_g(\text{reactants}) \]

Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate \(\Delta n_g\) for the formation of methane: \[ \Delta n_g = 1 - 2 = -1 \] 2. Substitute \(\Delta n_g = -1\) into the thermodynamic relation: \[ \Delta_f H^{\ominus} = \Delta_f U^{\ominus} + (-1)RT = \Delta_f U^{\ominus} - RT \] Since \(R > 0\) and \(T > 0\), the product \(RT\) is positive. Subtracting a positive quantity \(RT\) means: \[ \Delta_f H^{\ominus} < \Delta_f U^{\ominus} \]

Check and Final Answer
Because \(-393 - RT < -393\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), the value of \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) is strictly less than \(\Delta_f U^{\ominus}\). Final Answer: \(< \Delta_f U^{\ominus}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q07 - Free expansion of ideal gas under adiabatic conditions

questiontext.text: In an adiabatic process, no transfer of heat takes place between system and surroundings. Choose the correct option for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic condition from the following.

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Process conditions: Free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic conditions.

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
An adiabatic process has no heat exchange across the boundary: \(q = 0\).
Free expansion denotes expansion against vacuum (zero opposing external pressure): \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Expansion work: \(w = -\int p_{\text{ex}} dV\). Since \(p_{\text{ex}} = 0\), \(w = 0\).
2. First law of thermodynamics: \(\Delta U = q + w\).
3. Internal energy of an ideal gas: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, \(\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T\).

Step-by-Step Working
1. Since the process is adiabatic: \(q = 0\).
2. Since the gas expands freely into vacuum: \(w = 0\).
3. By the first law of thermodynamics: \[ \Delta U = q + w = 0 + 0 = 0 \]
4. For an ideal gas, since there are no intermolecular forces of attraction, expanding into a vacuum requires no work to separate gas molecules. With \(\Delta U = 0\), the temperature remains unchanged: \[ \Delta U = n C_v \Delta T = 0 \implies \Delta T = 0 \]

Check and Final Answer
All three state conditions are consistently zero: \(q = 0\), \(\Delta T = 0\), and \(w = 0\).
Final Answer: \(q = 0, \Delta T = 0, w = 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q08 - Comparison of reversible and irreversible compression work

questiontext.text: The pressure-volume work for an ideal gas can be calculated by using the expression \(w = -\int_{V_i}^{V_f} p_{ex} dV\). The work can also be calculated from the \(pV\)-plot by using the area under the curve within the specified limits. When an ideal gas is compressed (a) reversibly or (b) irreversibly from volume \(V_i\) to \(V_f\), choose the correct option.

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
An ideal gas undergoes compression from initial volume \(V_i\) to final volume \(V_f\) (where \(V_f < V_i\)) through: (a) a reversible path, and (b) an irreversible single-stage path against external pressure \(p_{\text{ex}}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Work done on the gas during compression is positive (\(w > 0\)). On an indicator diagram (\(pV\)-plot), the magnitude of compression work is given by the area under the process path between \(V_i\) and \(V_f\).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. In reversible compression, the external pressure matches the internal pressure at every instant (\(p_{\text{ex}} = p_{\text{int}} + dp\)). The work is: \[ w_{\text{rev}} = -\int_{V_i}^{V_f} p_{\text{int}} dV = nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_i}{V_f}\right) \] which is represented by the exact area under the smooth isothermal curve. 2. In irreversible compression in a single step, the opposing external pressure is instantaneously raised to the final pressure \(p_f\) (where \(p_f > p_i\)). The work done on the gas is: \[ w_{\text{irrev}} = -p_f (V_f - V_i) = p_f (V_i - V_f) \] which corresponds to the full rectangular area of height \(p_f\) and width \((V_i - V_f)\).

Step-by-Step Working
Because \(p_f\) is the highest pressure reached in the process, the rectangular area under the horizontal line \(p = p_f\) is strictly greater than the area under the curve connecting \(p_i\) to \(p_f\): \[ \text{Area}_{\text{irrev}} > \text{Area}_{\text{rev}} \] Therefore, the work done to compress the gas reversibly is less than the work required irreversibly: \[ w(\text{reversible}) < w(\text{irreversible}) \]

Check and Final Answer
Reversible compression requires the minimum possible work to compress a gas between two volumes. Hence, \(w(\text{reversible}) < w(\text{irreversible})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q09 - Entropy change during the freezing of water

questiontext.text: The entropy change can be calculated by using the expression \(\Delta S = \frac{q_{rev}}{T}\). When water freezes in a glass beaker, choose the correct statement amongst the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Entropy \(S\) is a measure of randomness or microscopic disorder of a thermodynamic system. Phase changes between solid, liquid, and gas alter entropy in accordance with changes in molecular positional freedom.

Evaluation of System and Surroundings
1. System (Water freezing to ice): Liquid water molecules possess greater positional randomness and freedom of motion than molecules locked in a rigid hexagonal ice crystal lattice. When water freezes, order increases, meaning the entropy of the system decreases (\(\Delta S_{\text{system}} < 0\)).
2. Surroundings: Freezing is an exothermic process. Latent heat of fusion is released by the freezing water to the surrounding environment (\(q_{\text{surr}} > 0\)). The addition of heat increases the thermal chaotic motion of molecules in the surroundings, resulting in an increase in entropy of the surroundings: \[ \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = \frac{q_{\text{rev, surr}}}{T} > 0 \]

Final Conclusion
When water freezes in a glass beaker, \(\Delta S\) (system) decreases but \(\Delta S\) (surroundings) increases.

answer.text: \(\Delta S\) (system) decreases but \(\Delta S\) (surroundings) remains the same.
\(\Delta S\) (system) decreases and \(\Delta S\) (surroundings) also decreases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q10 - Algebraic relation of enthalpies using Hess law

questiontext.text:
On the basis of thermochemical equations (a), (b) and (c), find out which of the algebraic relationships given in options (i) to (iv) is correct.

(a) \(\mathrm{C\,(graphite)} + \mathrm{O}_2\,(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2\,(\mathrm{g}); \quad \Delta_r H = x\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C\,(graphite)} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2\,(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}\,(\mathrm{g}); \quad \Delta_r H = y\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{CO}\,(\mathrm{g}) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2\,(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2\,(\mathrm{g}); \quad \Delta_r H = z\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Three thermochemical equations: \[ \text{Equation (a): } \mathrm{C(graphite)} + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g); \quad \Delta_r H_a = x \] \[ \text{Equation (b): } \mathrm{C(graphite)} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}(g); \quad \Delta_r H_b = y \] \[ \text{Equation (c): } \mathrm{CO}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g); \quad \Delta_r H_c = z \]

Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Hess's law of constant heat summation, if a chemical reaction can take place in several stages, the overall standard enthalpy change of the reaction is equal to the sum of the standard enthalpy changes for each intermediate step.

Step-by-Step Working
Add thermochemical equation (b) and equation (c): \[ \left[\mathrm{C(graphite)} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2(g)\right] + \left[\mathrm{CO}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2(g)\right] \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}(g) + \mathrm{CO}_2(g) \] Canceling the intermediate \(\mathrm{CO}(g)\) from both sides gives: \[ \mathrm{C(graphite)} + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g) \] This net chemical equation is identical to thermochemical equation (a).
Summing the corresponding enthalpies: \[ \Delta_r H_a = \Delta_r H_b + \Delta_r H_c \] \[ x = y + z \]

Check and Final Answer
Direct addition yields \(x = y + z\).
Final Answer: \(x = y + z\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q11 - Enthalpy comparison between bond formation and formation reaction

questiontext.text:
Consider the reactions given below. On the basis of these reactions find out which of the algebraic relations given in options (i) to (iv) is correct?

(a) \(\mathrm{C\,(g)} + 4\mathrm{H\,(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_4\,(\mathrm{g}); \quad \Delta_r H = x\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C\,(graphite, s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\,(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_4\,(\mathrm{g}); \quad \Delta_r H = y\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The enthalpy change of a reaction is related to the energy required to break bonds in reactant molecules and the energy released upon forming bonds in product molecules: \[ \Delta_r H = \sum \text{Bond Energy}_{\text{reactants}} - \sum \text{Bond Energy}_{\text{products}} \]

Evaluation of Both Reactions
In reaction (a), isolated gaseous carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms combine directly to form four \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds in \(\mathrm{CH}_4(g)\). No existing chemical bonds or lattice interactions in the reactants need to be broken; purely bond formation takes place, which releases the total bond dissociation energy of four \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds. In reaction (b), before \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) can be formed, energy must first be supplied to break the covalent \(\mathrm{H-H}\) bonds in \(\mathrm{H}_2(g)\) and to sublime solid graphite \(\mathrm{C}(s)\) into gaseous carbon atoms. Because the same four \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds are formed in both processes, but bond breaking occurs exclusively in the second reaction, the net heat release per mole is substantially greater in the first reaction.

Final Conclusion
Comparing the magnitudes of heat evolved, the relationship is \(x > y\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q12 - Possible sign of standard enthalpy of formation

questiontext.text: The enthalpies of elements in their standard states are taken as zero. The enthalpy of formation of a compound

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The standard molar enthalpy of formation \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) is defined as the enthalpy change accompanying the synthesis of one mole of a compound from its constituent elements in their standard reference states.

Evaluation of Exothermic and Endothermic Formations
Chemical synthesis from elemental forms may be either energetically downhill or uphill:

  • If the compound is more stable than its constituent elements, the reaction releases heat (exothermic), resulting in a negative enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} < 0\)), as seen in \(\mathrm{CO_2}(g)\) or \(\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\).
  • If the compound requires net energy to form because bond breaking in reactants exceeds the energy released by newly formed bonds, the reaction absorbs heat (endothermic), giving a positive enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} > 0\)), as seen in \(\mathrm{NO}(g)\) or \(\mathrm{C_2H_2}(g)\).

Final Conclusion
Therefore, the enthalpy of formation of a compound may be positive or negative.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q13 - Enthalpy of sublimation relation to fusion vapourisation

questiontext.text: Enthalpy of sublimation of a substance is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Sublimation is the direct phase transition of a substance from solid directly to vapour: \[ \text{Solid} \longrightarrow \text{Gas}; \quad \Delta_{\text{sub}} H \]

Step-by-Step Path Analysis
Because enthalpy is a state function, the net enthalpy change between two states is independent of the path taken. The direct transition from solid to gas can be envisioned as a two-stage sequential path: 1. Fusion (melting of solid into liquid): \[ \text{Solid} \longrightarrow \text{Liquid}; \quad \Delta_{\text{fus}} H \] 2. Vapourisation (boiling of liquid into gas): \[ \text{Liquid} \longrightarrow \text{Gas}; \quad \Delta_{\text{vap}} H \]
Adding the two equations yields: \[ \text{Solid} \longrightarrow \text{Gas} \]
By Hess's law of heat summation: \[ \Delta_{\text{sub}} H = \Delta_{\text{fus}} H + \Delta_{\text{vap}} H \]

Final Conclusion
The enthalpy of sublimation of a substance is equal to enthalpy of fusion + enthalpy of vapourisation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q14 - Incorrect statement regarding Gibbs free energy change

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G\) serves as the criterion for spontaneity and thermodynamic equilibrium at constant temperature and pressure:

  • For a spontaneous (feasible) process: \(\Delta G < 0\) (negative).
  • For a non-spontaneous process: \(\Delta G > 0\) (positive).
  • For a reversible process at dynamic equilibrium: \(\Delta G = 0\) (zero).

Evaluation of Statements
A spontaneous process must always have a negative Gibbs free energy change (\(\Delta G < 0\)). Therefore, asserting that \(\Delta G\) is positive for a spontaneous reaction directly violates the fundamental criterion of spontaneity.

Final Conclusion
The statement that is not correct is: \(\Delta G\) is positive for a spontaneous reaction.

answer.text: \(\Delta G\) is zero for a reversible reaction
\(\Delta G\) is positive for a spontaneous reaction
\(\Delta G\) is negative for a spontaneous reaction
\(\Delta G\) is positive for a non-spontaneous reaction

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q15 - Main domain and scope of macroscopic thermodynamics

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Classical thermodynamics is a macroscopic science that deals with properties of bulk matter rather than the microscopic behavior of individual molecules or systems consisting of only a few molecules.

Evaluation of Core Domains
1. Thermodynamics investigates the interconversion between various forms of energy (such as heat, work, chemical energy, and electrical energy) and formulates the quantitative laws governing these transformations. 2. The laws of thermodynamics apply strictly to systems at equilibrium or moving from one equilibrium state to another equilibrium state. 3. In contrast, thermodynamics does not deal with microscopic systems consisting of only a few molecules, nor does it address reaction rates or mechanisms (which are the province of kinetics).

Final Conclusion
Thermodynamics mainly deals with the interrelation of various forms of energy and their transformation from one form to another, and the system in equilibrium state or moving from one equilibrium state to another equilibrium state.

answer.text: interrelation of various forms of energy and their transformation from one form to another.
energy changes in the processes which depend only on initial and final states of the microscopic systems containing a few molecules.
how and at what rate these energy transformations are carried out.
the system in equilibrium state or moving from one equilibrium state to another equilibrium state.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q16 - Signs of heat and enthalpy in exothermic reaction

questiontext.text: In an exothermic reaction, heat is evolved, and system loses heat to the surrounding. For such system

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
According to the standard thermodynamic sign convention:

  • Heat absorbed by the system is positive (\(q > 0\)).
  • Heat released (evolved) by the system to the surroundings is negative (\(q < 0\)).

Enthalpy Relation at Constant Pressure
At constant pressure, the heat exchanged between the system and surroundings is equal to the enthalpy change of the reaction: \[ q_p = \Delta_r H \] Because the reaction is exothermic, heat leaves the system, meaning \(q_p\) must have a negative value (\(q_p < 0\)). Consequently, \(\Delta_r H\) must also be negative (\(\Delta_r H < 0\)).

Final Conclusion
For such a system, \(q_p\) will be negative and \(\Delta_r H\) will be negative.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q17 - Identification of naturally spontaneous physical chemical processes

questiontext.text: The spontaneity means, having the potential to proceed without the assistance of external agency. The processes which occur spontaneously are

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A spontaneous process is one that has a natural tendency to occur in a specific direction without requiring the continuous intervention of an external agency. Spontaneous changes are accompanied by an increase in total entropy (\(\Delta S_{\text{total}} > 0\)) and a decrease in Gibbs free energy (\(\Delta G < 0\)) at constant temperature and pressure.

Evaluation of Given Processes
1. Heat spontaneously flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature. Heat never flows spontaneously from a colder body to a warmer body. 2. Gas molecules move randomly and diffuse uniformly throughout the container. A gas contracting spontaneously into one corner is an unnatural, non-spontaneous process with extreme decrease in entropy. 3. A gas expanding into an evacuated or larger volume occurs spontaneously because spatial disorder increases (\(\Delta S > 0\)). 4. The combustion of carbon in oxygen: \[ \mathrm{C}(s) + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g); \quad \Delta H < 0 \] Once initiated, this reaction releases substantial energy and proceeds spontaneously to completion with a large negative Gibbs free energy change (\(\Delta G < 0\)).

Final Conclusion
The spontaneous processes are gas expanding to fill the available volume, and burning carbon in oxygen to give carbon dioxide.

answer.text: flow of heat from colder to warmer body.
gas in a container contracting into one corner.
gas expanding to fill the available volume.
burning carbon in oxygen to give carbon dioxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q18 - Reversible isothermal expansion work at different temperatures

questiontext.text:
For an ideal gas, the work of reversible expansion under isothermal condition can be calculated by using the expression \(w = -nRT \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}\).

A sample containing \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of an ideal gas is expanded isothermally and reversibly to ten times of its original volume, in two separate experiments. The expansion is carried out at \(300\text{ K}\) and at \(600\text{ K}\) respectively. Choose the correct option.

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Amount of ideal gas: \(n = 1.0\text{ mol}\).
Volume expansion ratio: \(\frac{V_f}{V_i} = 10\).
Temperatures of isothermal expansion: \(T_1 = 300\text{ K}\) and \(T_2 = 600\text{ K}\).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Reversible isothermal expansion work for an ideal gas: \[ w = -nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_f}{V_i}\right) \] 2. Change in internal energy of an ideal gas: \[ \Delta U = n C_v \Delta T \] In an isothermal process, temperature remains strictly constant throughout the expansion (\(\Delta T = 0\)), which implies \(\Delta U = 0\).

Step-by-Step Working
1. Compute the ratio of work done at \(600\text{ K}\) to work done at \(300\text{ K}\): \[ \frac{w(600\text{ K})}{w(300\text{ K})} = \frac{-n R (600) \ln(10)}{-n R (300) \ln(10)} = \frac{600}{300} = 2 \] Thus, the magnitude of work done at \(600\text{ K}\) is twice the work done at \(300\text{ K}\).
2. In both experiments, since the gas is ideal and the expansions are conducted isothermally: \[ \Delta U = 0 \text{ at } 300\text{ K} \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta U = 0 \text{ at } 600\text{ K} \]

Check and Final Answer
Both conditions hold: work done at \(600\text{ K}\) is twice the work done at \(300\text{ K}\), and \(\Delta U = 0\) in both cases.

answer.text: Work done at \(600\mathrm{K}\) is 20 times the work done at \(300\mathrm{K}\).
Work done at \(300\mathrm{K}\) is twice the work done at \(600\mathrm{K}\).
Work done at \(600\mathrm{K}\) is twice the work done at \(300\mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q19 - Enthalpy change and energy evolution in zinc combustion

questiontext.text:
Consider the following reaction between zinc and oxygen and choose the correct options out of the options given below :

\[ 2 \mathrm{Zn}(s) + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{ZnO}(s); \quad \Delta H = -693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \]

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Thermochemical reaction: \[ 2\mathrm{Zn}(s) + \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{ZnO}(s); \quad \Delta H = -693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \]

Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. The enthalpy change of a reaction is defined as: \[ \Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}} \] where \(H_{\text{products}} = H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{ZnO})\) and \(H_{\text{reactants}} = H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{Zn}) + H(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{O}_2)\).
2. When \(\Delta H < 0\), the reaction is exothermic, indicating that thermal energy is released (evolved) to the surroundings.

Step-by-Step Working
1. Since \(\Delta H = -693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), the process is exothermic and releases \(693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) of energy.
2. Expressing product enthalpy relative to reactants: \[ H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{ZnO}) - [H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{Zn}) + H(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{O}_2)] = -693.8\text{ kJ} \] \[ H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{ZnO}) = [H(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{Zn}) + H(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{O}_2)] - 693.8\text{ kJ} \] This confirms that the total enthalpy of two moles of \(\mathrm{ZnO}\) is less than the total enthalpy of two moles of \(\mathrm{Zn}\) and one mole of oxygen by \(693.8\text{ kJ}\).

Check and Final Answer
Energy is evolved (not absorbed) in the amount of \(693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), and the enthalpy of the product is less than that of the reactants by \(693.8\text{ kJ}\).
Final Answer: The enthalpy of two moles of \(\mathrm{ZnO}\) is less than the total enthalpy of two moles of \(\mathrm{Zn}\) and one mole of oxygen by \(693.8\text{ kJ}\), and \(693.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) energy is evolved in the reaction.
